examples.question: Which of these can I still apply to, and what is the deadline?
examples.answer:
Based on the sources I have, here's the status for each event:

## Junction 2026 — Yes, open, deadline **25 October 2026 (midnight, GMT+03)**
This is the only event in the set with an explicit, confirmed application deadline. It's stated identically on two of Junction's own surfaces:
- The official site: "Applications close - Midnight 25.10.2026 GMT +03"
- The application platform (hackjunction.app): "Registration Deadline: 25 Oct 2026, 22:55"

Both are organiser-controlled sources and agree, so this is accepted, not disputed. Apply at hackjunction.app/hackathons/junction-2026. Note: the separate travel-grant application deadline (6 September 2026) has already passed and is closed — don't confuse that with the main application deadline.

## BaselHack 2026 — Open, no stated deadline
BaselHack doesn't have an "application" step with a deadline — it's ticket-based registration via baselhack.ch/shop. As of the most recent update on their own blog, 50% of tickets had already been claimed, but no cutoff date is given. Practically, you can register until tickets run out or the event starts (30 Oct–1 Nov 2026).

## Odoo Hackathon #6 — Open, no stated deadline
No application or registration deadline is stated anywhere on Odoo's own event page. Registrations are currently open. Don't mistake the **14 November** date for a deadline to apply — that's the cancellation cutoff for getting your deposit back if you drop out, not an application deadline.

## CASSINI Hackathon #12 — Unclear for participants
The only application deadline mentioned in the sources concerns **local organisers**, and those applications are now closed. Nothing in the official CASSINI hackathon page or the Rules of Contest states a participant registration/application deadline — that would presumably be set by each of the 10 local organisers (Sofia, Prague, Espoo, Darmstadt, Dublin, Turin, Kaunas, Gdańsk, Bucharest, Ivano-Frankivsk) individually, but none of those local deadlines are stated in what I have. I can't tell you if or when participant applications close for this one.

## Power of Europe Amsterdam — Open by waitlist, no stated deadline
Entry is by waitlist request via the Luma listing, with acceptance by email. No precise application/registration deadline is stated on the public page. The event itself is on **18 October 2026**, so realistically any application would need to happen before then, but that's an inference from the event date, not a stated deadline.

---

**Bottom line:** Junction is the one with a firm, sourced deadline (25 Oct 2026). BaselHack, Odoo, and Power of Europe Amsterdam appear to still be accepting applicants but have no stated cutoff date. CASSINI's participant-facing deadline simply isn't stated anywhere I can see.

examples.question: If I go to a CASSINI local hackathon, can I win the 9,000 EUR?
examples.answer:
Not directly — attending a local hackathon alone doesn't put you in the running for the €9,000. Here's the distinction, straight from the sources:

**The €9,000 figure is real, but it's for the European Finals, not the local event.** The official CASSINI website states you can "compete for cash prizes up to 9,000 EUR (1st: 5,000, 2nd: 3,000, 3rd: 1,000) plus 6 months of mentoring" — but our dataset flags this as **superseded**, with a note that reading it on its own "suggests that turning up to your local hackathon puts you in the running for 9,000 EUR, and the Rules of Contest say otherwise."

**The EUSPA Rules of Contest (the authoritative document) say clearly:** "No monetary prize will be awarded in the first stage (Local Hackathons) by EUSPA. In case local organisers and/or other partners decide to award monetary prizes following the Local Hackathons and based on the outcome thereof, such prize shall not be confused with the Hackathon Prize nor considered in any way as a Prize awarded by EUSPA."

So the actual path to that money is:

1. You compete at one of the 10 local in-person hackathons (27–29 Nov 2026) — no EUSPA cash is on offer here.
2. Only the **top team from your city** advances to Stage 2, the European Finals (an online Demo Day).
3. Only at the Finals does EUSPA award the €5,000 / €3,000 / €1,000 (totaling €9,000), plus up to 100 hours of mentoring over 6 months for the three winning teams.

Local organisers *may* choose to hand out their own prizes at the local stage, but per the Rules, those are explicitly not EUSPA prizes and shouldn't be confused with the €9,000 pot.

I'd trust the Rules of Contest here (an "official-rules" document, EUSPA) over the marketing language on the main hackathons page — it's the source that actually governs the prize contest, and the dataset's verdict agrees.

examples.question: Which prizes are real cash?
examples.answer:
Here's the breakdown across the five events in the dataset, by whether the prize is actually cash:

**Confirmed cash — but only for a specific subset of participants**

- **CASSINI Hackathon #12 (EU Space for Peace and Resilience):** dataset marks this "yes," but with an important caveat. The official CASSINI site says you can "compete for cash prizes up to 9,000 EUR (1st: 5,000, 2nd: 3,000, 3rd: 1,000) plus 6 months of mentoring" — but this claim is flagged as **superseded**: it's only true of the European Finals, not the local hackathons. The official Rules of Contest (the authoritative document) state plainly that "No monetary prize will be awarded in the first stage (Local Hackathons) by EUSPA," and that any money a local organiser hands out separately "shall not be confused with the Hackathon Prize nor considered in any way as a Prize awarded by EUSPA." Only one team per city advances to the finals, so for everyone else there is no EUSPA cash at all. The finals prizes (€5k/€3k/€1k, €9,000 total) also come with up to 100 hours of mentoring for the three winning teams.

**Explicitly not cash**

- **Power of Europe Amsterdam:** prizes are partner credits, not cash — "Top 3 teams receive credits from partner companies (Orq AI, Mistral, Weaviate, Koyeb, Kilocode AI). First place: 7,800 EUR+ in combined credits; second place: 3,650+; third place: 2,550+." The dataset explicitly marks this "no" for cash — a 7,800 EUR headline with no cash in it.

**Not stated whether cash — headline figures exist but form is unconfirmed**

- **Junction 2026:** the official site states "€100,000 In prizes across the weekend. Full prize breakdown coming soon," but never says how much (if any) is cash. This is the largest prize figure in the dataset, and the dataset's note points out that "coming soon" has been sitting on the page since it was read — so treat the composition as unresolved, not confirmed cash.
- **BaselHack 2026:** the official site only says "Great prices for winners ... fantastic prize money" — no figure at all. The dataset verdict is "unresolved": there's no number on the official site, so any figure you might see elsewhere didn't come from BaselHack itself.
- **Odoo Hackathon #6:** described only as "fantastic prizes" evaluated by an Odoo expert panel — no value, cash-or-not status, or number of winners stated anywhere in official sources.

**Bottom line:** the only confirmed real cash prizes in this dataset are the CASSINI European Finals prizes (€5,000/€3,000/€1,000), and those apply only to the one team per city that advances beyond the local hackathon stage — not to local participants generally. Everything else is either explicitly non-cash (Power of Europe's credits) or a headline figure whose cash status is not stated (Junction, BaselHack, Odoo).

examples.question: What do the listing sites get wrong?
examples.answer:
Two aggregator/listing sites in this dataset get things wrong, and a third-party page (Wikipedia) goes stale in a similar way:

**hackathon.com — false negative, most severe failure**
On 20 September 2026 this aggregator stated: *"There is no upcoming hackathons found in 'Europe'"* (dataset source: hackathon.com, verdict: **incorrect**). A survey of five listing sites done the same day turned up fifteen candidate European events, five of which are actually tracked in this dataset. So "no results" from this site should never be read as "nothing is happening" — treat it as unreliable rather than authoritative (source_reliability, kbFmPO9HVpQh).

**dev.events — incomplete list that looks complete**
On the same date, dev.events listed only five European events for the whole continent: Turin (17–18 Oct), Bern (18–19 Oct), Basel/BaselHack (30 Oct–1 Nov), Odoo Hackathon #6 in Ramillies (20–22 Nov), and Barcelona (11–13 Dec) — dataset verdict **incorrect** on that list as a status claim. It omits Junction 2026 entirely, despite Junction being roughly 2,000 participants and €100,000 in prizes, running just three weeks after the last event on that list. The dangerous part, per the knowledge base, is that "no error message, no caveat, just missing coverage" makes the list look authoritative when it isn't (source_reliability).

Separately, dev.events' venue listing for Odoo Hackathon #6 says "Ramillies, Belgium" — this is marked **unresolved** rather than flatly wrong, because Grand-Rosière (the actual address, Rue des Bourlottes 9) is technically within the Ramillies municipality, but you can't navigate to a real location with just "Ramillies."

**Wikipedia — stale, not a listing site per se, but same failure pattern**
The "Junction (hackathon)" Wikipedia article, last edited 3 June 2026, still described the 2025 edition as of 20 September 2026, quoting dates of November 14–16. Junction 2026 actually runs 13–15 November — one day earlier. Verdict: **superseded**. The knowledge base calls this out as exactly the kind of near-miss that gets silently copied into other secondary sources.

**Trust hierarchy recommended by the knowledge base:**
1. Organiser's own site/official communications
2. This structured dataset (snapshot from 20 September 2026)
3. Third-party aggregators (dev.events, hackathon.com) — useful for discovery only, demonstrably incomplete/incorrect
4. Wikipedia — fine for background, not for current-edition logistics

Bottom line: don't take an aggregator's silence or absence-of-listing as proof an event doesn't exist or has been cancelled — in this dataset's snapshot, both major listing sites checked either under-reported or flatly denied events that were confirmed live on organisers' own pages.
